LoloBuy additional QC photos: how to request useful evidence

Turn a vague warehouse photo request into specific angles and details that support a shipping decision.

⌕

Product research and QC · 10 minute read

LoloBuy additional QC photos: write requests that answer one decision

Additional LoloBuy QC photos are most useful when the ordinary warehouse images leave one specific buying question unanswered. “Take more photos” is not a test plan. It gives the photographer no target, angle or reference point, and it may return another general view that looks different but proves nothing new.

The current LoloBuy warehouse record can separate ordinary inspection photos from fine or HD photos. Its quality report may also show the stored item, inspector information, weight or net weight, and dimensions or net dimensions when those fields are available. The extra-photo form allows a buyer to create individual photo instructions and attach a reference image. Its current limit and total are supplied by the live service configuration, so they should be checked in the account instead of copied from an older guide.

The practical goal is not to collect the largest gallery. It is to identify the smallest set of views that can change your decision: accept the item, request clarification, use an available return or exchange route, or prepare it for international shipping.

1. Audit the existing QC report before buying another photo

Open the exact warehouse item and match its item number to the original order. Compare the product title, source link, selected specification, quantity and seller image. Then inspect every ordinary photo at full size rather than relying on the thumbnail. A detail that looks missing in the thumbnail may already be visible after zooming or downloading the image.

Record what each existing image proves. A front view can confirm general shape and visible color. A label close-up can confirm printed size or model text. A top-down image can show the included pieces. A scale or measurement image can support a dimension. Mark uncertain points separately. This prevents paying for a duplicate view and helps you rank the remaining questions.

Read any quality warning attached to the stored item. A warehouse note about visible damage, a mismatch or a restricted characteristic deserves priority over cosmetic curiosity. Also compare the QC report’s weight and dimensions with the type of product ordered. An unexpected figure is a reason to ask what was measured, not immediate proof that the product is wrong.

2. Turn the seller listing into a verification sheet

Before writing the request, save the product listing details that mattered when you ordered: selected color, size, model, material claim, included accessories, printed label, pattern placement and seller measurement chart. Marketplace pages can change, so preserve a dated screenshot of the relevant section for your own evidence.

Build a two-column check. On the left, write the seller claim. On the right, write the photograph that could visibly test it. “Size 42” maps to a close-up of the size label. “Black hardware” maps to a well-lit close-up of the buckle or zipper. “Includes two straps” maps to one top-down image showing every included part in the same frame.

Some claims do not map to a reliable photo. A picture cannot establish authenticity, chemical composition, long-term durability, scent, battery health or internal construction. Do not waste an extra-photo slot asking the photographer to prove something the camera cannot demonstrate.

3. Use one question per photo instruction

The LoloBuy fine-photo form organizes requests as separate photo entries. Use that structure. Each entry should contain one subject, one angle and one visible reference. A useful instruction looks like: “Photograph the inside size label straight on, with all text in focus.” Another might be: “Place a ruler across the insole from heel to longest toe and show both ends of the ruler.”

Avoid combining several unrelated tasks in one sentence. “Show the label, stitching, box, sole and accessories” creates uncertainty about which detail should fill the frame. If each detail could change your decision, give it its own instruction. If it cannot, leave it out.

Use physical locations rather than vague adjectives. Replace “check the logo” with “close-up of the embroidered chest logo, camera parallel to the fabric.” Replace “show quality” with “close-up of the left side seam from armpit to hem under neutral light.” The photographer can follow a location and angle; “quality” is a judgment.

4. Attach a reference image when words may be ambiguous

The current request form supports an optional reference image for an individual photo instruction. Use it to circle the exact area, demonstrate the intended measuring line or show which accessory should be present. Crop the reference so the requested detail is obvious.

A reference image is guidance, not evidence that the warehouse item must look identical. Lighting, lens distance and product variation can change appearance. If color is important, ask for a neutral-light image beside a familiar neutral reference, but do not treat screen color as a calibrated measurement.

Do not upload a collage full of arrows and several questions. One cropped reference paired with one written request is easier to execute and audit. Remove personal information, order data from other customers and unrelated images before attaching it.

5. Choose product-specific photo requests

For footwear, prioritize the size label, both shoes together, outsole condition, toe shape and a relevant internal or external measurement. If the ordinary photos suggest asymmetry, request the left and right shoes aligned from the same angle. A photo cannot confirm comfort or fit on your foot.

For clothing, ask for the neck or care label, front and back laid flat, the specific print or embroidery, and only the measurements needed to compare with the seller chart. State the measurement endpoints: pit to pit, shoulder seam to shoulder seam, waistband flat or total garment length. “Measure the shirt” is too vague.

For bags and accessories, request the interior, closure, hardware, strap attachment, label and included parts that matter to you. If damage is suspected, ask for one wider image locating the area and one close-up showing its surface. The pair provides context and detail.

For electronics or mechanical items, photographs can show model labels, ports, plugs, visible condition and included accessories. They cannot prove battery capacity, hidden circuitry or sustained operation unless a separately described test service exists and its result is documented. Do not infer functional testing from a product being photographed.

6. Separate visible evidence from conclusions

A sharp photo can show that printed text is present, stitching appears continuous in the visible area or a surface has a mark. It does not prove why the mark occurred, whether a material is genuine or whether an item will perform as advertised. Describe what the image shows before deciding what it means.

Use three labels in your notes: confirmed, unclear and not photographable. Confirmed means the requested detail is readable in the image. Unclear means glare, blur, angle or obstruction prevents a decision. Not photographable means the claim requires a test, document or expert method beyond a warehouse photo.

If the response is unclear, do not simply repeat the same instruction. Explain the failure: “The label text is blurred; please retake straight on with the entire label in focus.” This creates a traceable correction rather than a second ambiguous request.

7. Request photos before the item enters a parcel

The fine-photo action is associated with an eligible warehouse item. The current interface does not offer it in every item state, including after certain parcel, return, cancellation or completion stages. Finish your photo review while the item is still available in the warehouse and before submitting it into an international package.

An open value-service record can also have its own payment, pending, cancelled or finished status. Check that record rather than assuming the photo request is complete when the order is created. Review the delivered images and resolve any relevant seller-return question before selecting the item for parcel submission.

Do not assume that requesting a photo extends a seller’s return window or the item’s storage eligibility. Those are separate processes. Check the live account status and any applicable seller or platform conditions when timing affects your decision.

8. Build a decision file, not a photo collection

Keep the order number, warehouse item number, selected SKU, seller-listing screenshot, original QC images, extra-photo instructions and returned images together. Name each requested photo by its question, such as “size-label,” “insole-length” or “left-seam-mark.” A numbered folder makes it much easier to explain a mismatch to support.

After the extra images arrive, write one outcome for each question. If the size label matches, close that issue. If a measurement differs, record the seller chart, photographed measurement and measurement method. If a visible defect matters, preserve both the context image and close-up before opening any available return or exchange workflow.

Final LoloBuy additional QC photos checklist

Start with the existing quality report. Match the item number, SKU and seller listing; inspect ordinary photos; note recorded weight and dimensions; and read any quality warning. Convert only the remaining decision-critical claims into photo requests.

For every additional photo, specify one subject, one angle and one reference point. Attach one cropped example when needed. Request measurements with exact endpoints, separate visible facts from conclusions, and never treat photographs as proof of authenticity, hidden function or material composition. Complete this work before parcel submission, then save the full evidence set with the item record. Fewer targeted photos usually produce a better buying decision than a larger gallery of general views.
